newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss to consider compensating victims of Nazis.
newsitem.headline: Swiss to consider compensating victims of Nazis.

text.p: Swiss bankers and politicians, embarrassed by allegations the Alpine country profited from the Holocaust, are considering whether to create a fund for victims of Nazism as a gesture of reconciliation.

Financiers and politicians interviewed this week said debate was just starting in parliament and bankers were divided, but that a fund was one option for responding to months of Jewish-led attacks on the Swiss financial role in World War Two.
"The question has been asked directly and now we must give some kind of answer," said Victor Ruffy, chairman of the foreign policy committee of the lower house of parliament.

Ruffy was referring to the latest calls for a Holocaust fund, which came this week from World Jewish Congress (WJC) vice-president and British parliamentarian Greville Janner, and from the Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities (SIG).

"For the banks, I can only say that we will certainly not wipe Janner's proposal off the table. This must be discussed," said Heinrich Schneider, deputy general secretary of the Swiss Bankers Association.

Janner's call for a quick payment to Nazi victims added to pressure for Switzerland to act rather than wait for an international audit of Swiss banks and a major probe of how much Jewish wealth and Nazi loot may have came into Switzerland.

The Swiss set up the probes in response to mounting allegations that Swiss banks hoarded accounts left by Holocaust victims, accepted Nazi loot and the Swiss National Bank cynically profited from buying stolen Nazi gold.
Janner named no figures, but other WJC officials have suggested an amount around 100 million to 200 million Swiss francs ($157.8 million).

"Certainly, the pressure is growing," said Hans Baer, Switzerland's most prominent Jewish banker and a member of the committee set up by Swiss banks and world Jewish groups to sweep for accounts left dormant by Holocaust victims.

But he said there was no way to decide how much Switzerland might put into a potential fund for Nazi victims until the audit commision, headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker, finishes its work in mid-1998.
"We do not know the parameters yet of how much Jewish and other refugee money was put here. Once one knows the parameters, then I think one can certainly talk about this issue (a fund)," he said.
Baer echoed other Swiss leader by saying he believed Switzerland had shown it was serious about compensating any past wrongs by setting up three separate probes of war-time finances.

Besides the Volcker commission auditing banks, a bank ombudsman is coordinating searches by Holocaust heirs for lost accounts and parliament is due next month to approve a broad review by independent historians of war-time wealth bunkered in Switzerland.
One concern cited by Swiss leaders is whether their critics, including the WJC in New York and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, will stop their attacks if a compensation fund is set up.

They note that WJC leaders still accuse Switzerland of hiding Holocaust accounts even after the banks gave unprecedented access to their vaults to the Volcker commission, which was set up with the WJC as a partner.

Another concern is whether any payment would be taken as an expression of guilt in two multi-billion dollar lawsuits filed in New York against Swiss banks in the name of heirs of Holocuast victims. ($1=1.2670 Swiss Franc)
